Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

tidystata 0.3.0

Breaking changes

  • The package is renamed from statart to tidystata. Use library(tidystata) and tidystata:: in place of library(statart) and statart::.

  • The bundled starwars dataset is removed; use dplyr::starwars. dplyr 1.1.4 or later is now required, so every supported dplyr ships the same data. lifeexp is rebuilt from World Bank World Development Indicators (CC BY 4.0) with the same columns, labels and countries; its values are the World Bank’s current 1998 figures, and safewater is now the 2000 share using safely managed drinking water. See the installed DATA-PROVENANCE.md.

  • tidystata now focuses on exploring and preparing data. read_data(), write_data(), esttab(), codebook_detail(), tidy_coef(), the regression wrappers (regress(), regress_data(), regress_coef(), regress_stat()) and the plotting helpers (s_plot(), s_ggsave()) are removed. s_time() is renamed to timer(). The migration guide lists direct alternatives.

  • R 4.1.0 or later is now required. Persistent preview formatting requires tibble >= 3.2.0 and pillar >= 1.9.0, as dplyr >= 1.1.4 does. readr >= 1.4.0 is required for scientific notation and parsing diagnostics in as_numeric() and destring().

  • Required dependencies fall from 33 to 16 packages. Rich table output now needs the optional flextable package, and Rfast is no longer used.

  • Table-producing helpers preserve a base data.frame, tibble or data.table input container, including empty results and tables inside list outputs. Summaries and inventories are ungrouped. Newly constructed tables do not keep arbitrary subclass metadata.

  • fre() and fre2() default to .type = "auto". Request .type = "tibble" for a tibble or .type = "flextable" for rich output. An empty selection in fre2(..., .type = "flextable") is now an error instead of silently returning a tibble.

  • summ() and tabstat() sort .by groups like tab() (.sort = TRUE: factor levels, ascending keys, missing keys last) and drop the name column when exactly one variable is summarised (.name = FALSE). Use .sort = FALSE or .name = TRUE for the previous layout.

  • summ() and tabstat() return calendar spread statistics (sd, se, mad, iqr) as difftime columns with one unit per column, so rows can be compared and used in arithmetic. .duration_format no longer affects the output. With .type = "table", calendar spreads are numbers in days (Dates) or seconds, the unit is appended to type (for example "date [days]"), and numeric values in shared text columns are rounded to seven significant digits.

  • xtile() (formerly cut_quantile()) follows Stata’s xtile rule: equal values stay in the same group and distinct values are never merged, so a 0/1 dummy gives two groups. When ties leave fewer than n groups, occupied groups are numbered consecutively with a warning. Untied data give the same results as before. Inside a grouped data mask without labels, it returns integer codes, because group-specific interval labels cannot be combined.

  • s_select(), and therefore tab(), summ() and related functions, computes expressions that use columns instead of first trying them as selections: half = y / x previously selected column y. Named constants (one = 1) create constant columns, and misspelled or out-of-range selections are an error listing every unmatched name. Computed expressions run once.

  • timer() reports the elapsed time on failure by default (on_error = TRUE); the original error object and call are untouched.

  • row_min() and row_max() keep the common input type: logical inputs return logical values and integer inputs return integers, instead of always returning doubles. They also support character values, ordered factors and calendar, duration, measured, labelled and integer64 values. Numeric constants behave as in pmin() and pmax(): row_min(x, 0.5) caps x, and constants never fill all-missing rows.

  • mvdecode() (formerly na_if_value()) treats several codes as a set, like Stata’s mv(-98 -99), instead of comparing them elementwise as dplyr::na_if() does. A single code works as before.

  • Enumerated options (.type, .wt_type, .group_order, method, unit, relationship, style) are checked with rlang::arg_match(), so they must be spelled in full. A mistyped value suggests the intended one.

Lifecycle changes

  • Functions carry their Stata names, and the earlier names stay as quiet aliases on the same help pages: xtile() (cut_quantile()), capture() (s_try()), ds(.type = "table") (ds_as_column(), names_as_column()), mvdecode() and mvencode() (na_if_value(), value_if_na()), and destring() and decode() (as_numeric(), as_character()). New aliases are pct() for pc(), xtab() for tab2(), s_tag() for is_first() and tab_gen() for as_dummy().

  • s_match(), s_type() and s_unit() are deprecated in favour of varlist(), var_type() and var_unit(). They still work, with a lifecycle warning.

  • Arguments follow one naming rule: options after a ... that takes columns or expressions are dotted, and functions without ... use plain names. destring(), decode(), var_type(), var_unit(), na_if_value(), value_if_na() and timer() take x (not .x); capture() and set_seed() take x (not .fn); var_type(abbr), timer(on_error), na_if_value(value) and value_if_na(value) drop their dots; s_merge() takes keep, assert, generate and report; and varlist() takes ignore_case. The old names keep working with a deprecation warning.

  • summ() and tabstat() replace .na.rm with .missing (with the opposite value, default TRUE), matching is_first() and row_nvals(), and replace .mode with .type (same "list" and "table" values).

New features

Coming from Stata

  • New findit() gives the R equivalent of a Stata command: the tidystata function where one exists, and the standard package otherwise. Type one word bare (findit(reg)) or quote longer code (findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)")). Stata’s minimum abbreviations work, and unmatched text falls back to a keyword search. R function names work too (findit(left_join)), listing the Stata idioms they replace. findit() alone lists all of about 410 idioms. New “Coming from Stata” articles, in English and Chinese, show the entries by topic.

Tabulation

  • New tab2() cross-tabulates two variables, like Stata’s tab x y, and fre2() adds the total row and column. With three or more variables it returns every pairwise table as a named list, as Stata’s tab2 does. .by returns one cross-table per group, like by g: tab x y.

  • tab2(.chi2 = TRUE) reports Pearson’s chi-square, its p-value and Cramer’s V, like tab x y, chi2 V, and stores them in attr(x, "chi2").

  • tab() and tab1() gain .total: tab(.total = TRUE) equals fre() and tab1(.total = TRUE) equals fre1().

  • tab(), tab1(), fre(), fre1(), tab2(), summ() and tabstat() gain .wt and .wt_type, like Stata’s [fweight] and [aweight]. Weighted summaries follow Stata’s formulas, including its weighted percentile rule. xtile() gains wt for weighted cutpoints.

  • fre(), tab1() and fre1() accept atomic vectors, like tab().

  • Grouped frequencies gain .group_order = "frequency", independent of within-group .desc sorting.

Summaries

  • New pwcorr() returns a tidy table of pairwise correlations with n and p-values, like pwcorr, sig obs, with .method = "spearman", .by, weights and .wide = TRUE for Stata’s lower-triangle matrix.

  • New misstable() summarises missing values by variable, like misstable summarize, or missing patterns with .patterns = TRUE.

  • summ() and tabstat() accept any percentile p0 to p100 (including decimals such as p2.5), the aliases missing, p25, p50 and p75, and a numeric sum. Only requested statistics are calculated.

  • summ() and tabstat() gain .sort and .drop_empty. With .keep_all = TRUE, character and list columns keep counts and unique values. hms times of day form their own time family.

Checking and combining data

  • New isid() checks that columns uniquely identify the rows, like Stata’s isid.

  • New duplicates_report(), duplicates_tag(), duplicates_list() and duplicates_drop() follow Stata’s duplicates subcommands.

  • New assert(), like Stata’s assert, checks conditions on every row and returns the data invisibly, so it fits in a pipe.

  • New s_merge() joins like Stata’s merge: it checks the key relationship ("1:1", "m:1", "1:m"), prints a matched/unmatched report and adds a .merge factor, with keep, assert and generate options.

Generating variables

  • New std() and pc(), like Stata’s egen std() and egen pc(), use each group’s statistics in grouped mutate() or with .by.

  • New as_dummy() creates one 0/1 column per observed category, like tabulate x, generate(x_).

  • New is_first(), like egen tag(), flags the first row of each group.

  • New s_lag(), s_lead() and s_diff(), like Stata’s L.x, F.x and D.x after xtset, find values by time rather than row position, so gaps give missing values. They support Dates by period (unit), date-times, tsibble and zoo period classes and ordered factors.

  • New row_nvals(), like egenmore’s egen rownvals(), counts distinct values in each row.

  • New tostring(), like Stata’s tostring, gives values as text, keeping codes rather than value labels.

  • xtile() gains method = "rank" for balanced groups that may split ties.

Selecting and previewing

  • New preview_table() keeps a full table while displaying head/tail or evenly spaced rows; the setting persists through supported dplyr and tidyr operations. unpreview_table() removes it.

  • New print_all(), like Stata’s list, prints every row and column. New s_print() prints the first and last rows, evenly spaced rows or every row through one style argument.

  • print_headtail(), print_interval(), slice_headtail() and slice_interval() are restored and accept sf data.

  • ds() gains .type = "table", returning the names as a one-column table.

  • set_seed(123) also works on its own, like set seed 123.

  • variables_search() also searches variable labels.

Minor improvements and bug fixes

  • tab(), tab1(), fre() and fre1() check that .desc is TRUE or FALSE before tabulating; a vector or NA previously failed inside the sorting step, and aborted R 4.1. row_var() now matches stats::var() exactly on platforms without extended precision, such as Apple Silicon.

  • The plain example scripts and the migration guide are no longer installed with the package. The scripts are in the repository’s examples/ folder and the guide is the website’s Migration guide article.

  • SPSS user-defined missing codes and ranges (haven::labelled_spss()) are treated as missing throughout: in pwcorr(), misstable(), std(), pc(), is_first(.missing = FALSE), as_dummy(), the panel operators, codebook() and mvencode(), as summ() and tab() already did.

  • Errors, warnings and messages use cli. Errors name the function you called, describe the problem in one sentence and give hints as bullets. Code that matched the old wording may need updating; results are unchanged.

  • Examples, vignettes and README use the native pipe |>. %>% is still exported.

  • pwcorr() excludes zero-weight values, avoids overflow with very large weights or scales, and rejects explicitly selected matrix or array columns. Analytic weights in tabulations and summaries normalize safely within each group.

  • duplicates_list() preserves grouping and errors when .row or .dup_group already exists.

  • summ() and tabstat() keep numeric and logical columns with no observed values, including zero-row inputs; combine numeric and calendar summaries in .type = "table" without type conflicts; display datetimes in their own time zone and infinite Dates as Inf/-Inf; skip calendar variables with a warning when sum, skew or kurtosis is requested; and rename grouping keys that collide with summary columns, with a message.

  • A piped vector (x |> summ()) is named value. .by given a computed expression explains that it selects columns, instead of “object not found”.

  • tab(), tab1(), fre() and fre1() calculate statistics and totals within each group, keep missing group keys and place missing categories last. An explicit .by replaces inherited groups. List columns are counted, and selecting no variables returns an empty result.

  • tab2() and fre2() order columns by value or factor level with missing last, support blank column categories, keep categories that match variable names and report ambiguous name collisions; fre2() rejects a column category "total".

  • codebook() returns one inventory of the selected columns even for grouped input, and counts missing list elements and structured columns consistently.

  • Row helpers return vectors consistently, handle empty and all-missing rows, use sample variance and standard deviation, keep calendar, duration and measured units where arithmetic is defined, and can use grouping columns inside grouped mutate(). row_mean(), row_median(), row_var(), row_sd(), row_min(), row_max() and row_sum() accept na.rm.

  • var_type() recognizes measured vectors, and var_unit() returns their units, including compound units such as m/s. Custom and structured type descriptions are kept instead of truncated.

  • destring() parses character input while keeping its length and missing positions and exposing parsing warnings. decode() handles labelled vectors without value labels, including tagged missing values.

  • varlist() combines space-separated numeric-range patterns correctly and gives a direct error for non-character patterns.

  • cut_length() rejects invalid interval counts before calculating breaks. Help clarifies that a scalar cut_breaks() value is an interior cutpoint.

  • s_select() returns the first successful operation without rerunning it and keeps its warnings.

  • na_if_value() and value_if_na() give actionable messages when required arguments are missing; value_if_na() fills SPSS user-missing codes.

  • browse() returns the viewed data invisibly with their class preserved.

  • Optional data.table operations explain the missing dependency when needed.

  • Two vignettes cover a short workflow and the output-container, grouping and missing-value conventions.

Performance

Results are unchanged; only the time taken to compute them is shorter.

  • Row helpers are 2-5 times faster on large data (for example, row_unique() on 1,000,000 rows fell from about 300 ms to 55 ms), and row_sum() and row_mean() no longer copy the columns into a matrix.

  • summ() with many groups is much faster: .detail = TRUE over 10,000 groups fell from about 1,060 ms to 240 ms.

  • tab(), fre() and tab2() with many groups are faster, especially with weights (weighted tab() over 10,000 groups: 200 ms to 80 ms).

  • s_merge(), destring(), pwcorr(), grouped xtile() and codebook() also do less work.
